intro: How many buttons fit in a jar? How many cups of lemonade can you sell in a weekend? Big numbers are everywhere. This unit shows you how big numbers are built. Every number up to 1,000 is made of hundreds, tens and ones.

You will read and write numbers to 1,000. You will compare them with >, < and =. You will count by 5s, 10s and 100s. Then you will add and subtract big numbers by trading tens and ones. And you will explain why your way works.
bigQuestion: How do hundreds, tens and ones let us count, compare, add and subtract numbers up to 1,000?

timeline.t: Count buttons one by one and lose your place
Make groups of ten so counting goes faster
Ten groups of ten make one hundred
Ten hundreds fill the jar: one thousand
Write a number as hundreds, tens and ones
Add cups sold: tens with tens, ones with ones
Trade ten ones for a ten when there are too many
Trade a ten for ten ones so you can subtract
Add and subtract hundreds with drawings
Explain your strategy and check it another way

a number written as hundreds plus tens plus ones, like 300 + 40 + 7
bigger than; the sign is >
to count by jumps of the same size, like 5, 10, 15, 20

test.q: What number is 6 hundreds, 0 tens and 4 ones?

test.why: 2 hundreds is 200. 7 tens is 70. 5 ones is 5. So 200 + 70 + 5.
The hundreds tie. 4 tens is less than 8 tens. So 348 < 384.
56 ends in 6. It makes 28 pairs with none left over. 56 is even.
655 + 100 = 755. The hundreds digit goes from 6 to 7.
6 + 7 = 13. Trade ten ones for a ten. 2 + 4 + 1 = 7 tens. So 73.
Trade: 8 tens and 11 ones. 11 − 5 = 6. 8 − 3 = 5 tens. So 56.

write.prompt: Solve 53 − 27. Show each step with tens and ones. Explain why you traded a ten. Then check your answer by adding.
tips: Show the trade: 4 tens and 13 ones.
Say why: 3 ones is not enough to take away 7.

title: Place Value to 1,000

chapters.title: Hundreds, Tens and Ones
chapters.bigQuestion: How can three little digits stand for a number as big as 1,000?

story.title: The Button Jar
story.kicker: A big jar of buttons sits on a shelf. Nobody knows how many are inside.
paragraphs: Mrs. Diaz keeps a big glass jar on the shelf. It is full of buttons. Red ones, blue ones, tiny white ones. One day she asks the class a question. How many buttons are in the jar? Everyone guesses. Ten! A hundred! A million!

Two friends, Kai and Rosa, pour the buttons out. Kai starts to count. One, two, three. At forty-two, someone sneezes. Kai loses his place. He has to start again. Rosa has an idea. Let's make groups of ten, she says.

They make piles of ten buttons. Ten piles of ten make one hundred. They put each hundred in a paper cup. Soon the table is covered with cups. They stop and count the cups. Ten cups. That is ten hundreds. Ten hundreds make one thousand!

Mrs. Diaz smiles. You did not count 1,000 buttons one by one, she says. You counted hundreds, tens and ones. That is how big numbers work. Every big number is just groups. Groups of one hundred, groups of ten and some left over.
story.think: Why did making groups of ten help Kai and Rosa count faster than counting one by one?

lessons.title: Hundreds, Tens and Ones
lessons.mainIdea: A three-digit number is made of hundreds, tens and ones.
reading: Think of base-ten blocks. A little cube is one. A rod of ten cubes is a *ten*. A flat square of ten rods is a *hundred*. A hundred has 100 little cubes in it.
Look at 347. The 3 is in the hundreds place. It means 3 hundreds, or 300. The 4 is in the tens place. It means 4 tens, or 40. The 7 is in the ones place. It means 7 ones.
The place tells you the value. A 3 in the hundreds place is 300. A 3 in the ones place is just 3. Same digit, different job. Always ask: which place is it in?

words.d: a group of ten tens, or 100 ones
a group of ten ones
the spot a digit sits in, which tells its value

look.title: Blocks on the Table
look.text: Picture 2 flat hundreds on the table. Next to them are 5 rods of ten. Next to the rods are 6 little cubes. Count the hundreds. Count the tens. Count the ones. Say the number the blocks show.
look.prompt: What number do the blocks show? Say how many hundreds, tens and ones.

check.q: In 582, what does the 5 stand for?
check.why: The 5 is in the hundreds place. It means 5 hundreds, or 500.

check.q: How many tens make one hundred?
check.why: Ten rods of ten make one flat hundred. 10 tens = 100.

check.q: Which number has 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 9 ones?
check.why: 4 hundreds is 400. 0 tens is 0. 9 ones is 9. 400 + 0 + 9 = 409.

lessons.title: Expanded Form
lessons.mainIdea: Expanded form breaks a number into hundreds plus tens plus ones.
reading: You can stretch a number out. This is called *expanded form*. Take 347. It has 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 7 ones. So 347 = 300 + 40 + 7.
Try 615. The 6 means 600. The 1 means 10. The 5 means 5. Write it as 600 + 10 + 5. Add it back up. 600 + 10 = 610. Then 610 + 5 = 615. It matches.
Watch out for zeros. In 508, the 0 means 0 tens. So 508 = 500 + 8. Some students write 500 + 0 + 8. That is fine too. Just do not write 58!

words.d: a number written as hundreds plus tens plus ones, like 300 + 40 + 7

look.title: Stretch It Out
look.text: Rosa has 263 buttons. She puts 2 hundreds in cups. She puts 6 tens in rows. She keeps 3 loose. Write the cups, the rows and the loose buttons as an adding sentence.

check.why: 7 hundreds is 700. 2 tens is 20. 9 ones is 9. So 700 + 20 + 9.
306 has 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 6 ones. So 300 + 6.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Say the hundreds, then the tens and ones, to read a number up to 1,000.
reading: To read 347, say the hundreds first. Three hundred. Then say the rest like a two-digit number. Forty-seven. Three hundred forty-seven. Do not say 'and' in the middle.
Now write a number from words. Five hundred twelve. Five hundred is 500. Twelve is 12. Put them together: 512. Be careful with 'twelve'. It is one ten and two ones.
One *thousand* is written 1,000. It is ten hundreds. The comma helps your eye. Nine hundred ninety-nine is 999. One more makes 1,000.

words.d: one of the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers
ten hundreds, written 1,000

look.title: Numbers in Words
look.cite: Number names and the digits that write them
look.prompt: Which number in the table has a 0 in the tens place? Which have a 0 in the ones place?

check.q: How do you write six hundred forty-two?
check.why: Six hundred is 600. Forty-two is 42. 600 + 42 = 642.
The 8 is 800. Then 0 tens and 3 ones. Eight hundred three.
999 + 1 = 1,000. Ten hundreds make one thousand.

lessons.title: Which Number Is Bigger?
lessons.mainIdea: Compare the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones.
reading: Kai has 348 buttons. Rosa has 352. Who has more? Let's *compare*. Look at the hundreds first. Both have 3 hundreds. It is a tie. Move to the tens.
Kai has 4 tens. Rosa has 5 tens. 5 tens is more than 4 tens. So 352 is bigger than 348. You do not even need the ones. The tens settled it.
A common mistake is to look at the ones first. 348 has an 8. 352 has a 2. But 8 ones is only 8. One ten is worth 10. Bigger places win. Start on the left.

words.d: to look at two numbers and tell which is bigger, smaller or the same

look.title: Two Towers
look.text: Look at two towers of blocks. Tower A has 5 hundreds and 1 ten. Tower B has 4 hundreds, 9 tens and 9 ones. Tower B looks busy with all those blocks. But count the hundreds. Which tower is really worth more?
look.prompt: Which tower is worth more, and what place did you check to decide?

check.why: Both have 4 hundreds. 8 tens is more than 7 tens. 481 is bigger.
209 has 2 hundreds. 190 has only 1 hundred. 190 is smaller.

check.q: To compare 635 and 638, which place do you need to check last?
check.why: The hundreds tie at 6. The tens tie at 3. The ones decide it. 8 is more than 5, so 638 is bigger.

lessons.title: The Signs >, < and =
lessons.mainIdea: Use > for greater than, < for less than and = for equal to.
reading: Three signs help you compare. The sign > means *greater than*. The sign < means *less than*. The sign = means *equal to*. The open side of > or < always faces the bigger number.
Compare 352 and 348. 352 is greater. Write 352 > 348. Now flip it. 348 is less than 352. Write 348 < 352. Both say the same thing.
What about 500 and 500? They are the same. Write 500 = 500. Think of the sign as a hungry mouth. It opens to eat the bigger number.

words.d: bigger than; the sign is >
smaller than; the sign is <
the same amount; the sign is =

look.title: Feed the Mouth
look.text: Kai writes 720 ? 702. He is not sure which sign goes in the middle. Both have 7 hundreds. Look at the tens. 720 has 2 tens. 702 has 0 tens. Which number is bigger? Which way should the mouth open?
look.prompt: Which sign belongs in 720 ? 702: greater than, less than or equal to?

check.why: The hundreds tie. 1 ten is less than 5 tens. So 415 < 451.
The sign > means greater than. 9 tens beats 0 tens, so 890 is greater.
300 + 40 is 340. So 340 = 340. They are equal.

lessons.title: Counting by 5s, 10s and 100s
lessons.mainIdea: Skip counting adds the same amount each time: 5, 10 or 100.
reading: To *skip count* means to count by jumps. Count by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Count by 10s: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Count by 100s: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500.
You can start anywhere. Start at 340 and count by 10s. 340, 350, 360, 370. Only the tens digit changes. Start at 340 and count by 100s. 340, 440, 540. Only the hundreds digit changes.
Skip counting is fast. Rosa has 6 cups of 100 buttons. She counts 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600. Six jumps of 100 is 600. Much faster than counting one by one.

words.d: to count by jumps of the same size, like 5, 10, 15, 20

look.title: Counting Cups of 100
look.cite: Rosa's button cups, 100 buttons in each cup
look.prompt: How many buttons would 7 cups hold? Keep the pattern going.

check.why: 45 + 5 = 50. Each jump adds 5.

check.q: Count by 10s from 570: 570, 580, ___. What comes next?
check.why: 580 + 10 = 590. Only the tens digit changes.
450 + 100 = 550. The hundreds digit goes up by 1.

lessons.title: 100 More and 100 Less
lessons.mainIdea: Adding or taking away 100 changes only the hundreds digit.
reading: What is 100 *more* than 462? Add one hundred. The hundreds digit goes from 4 to 5. The tens and ones stay the same. 462 + 100 = 562.
What is 100 *less* than 462? Take one hundred away. The hundreds digit goes from 4 to 3. 462 − 100 = 362. The 6 and the 2 do not move.
The same trick works for 10. 10 more than 462 is 472. 10 less than 462 is 452. Only the tens digit changes. Be careful near 9 tens: 10 more than 495 is 505.

words.d: a bigger amount; 100 more means add 100
a smaller amount; 100 less means take away 100

look.title: The Elevator Game
look.text: Pretend a tall building has floors numbered like our numbers. You are on floor 384. The up button takes you up 100 floors. The down button takes you down 100 floors. Press up once. Where are you? Now start again at 384 and press down twice.
look.prompt: What floor is 100 more than 384? What floor is 200 less than 384?

check.why: 738 + 100 = 838. Only the hundreds digit changes, from 7 to 8.
520 − 100 = 420. The hundreds digit drops from 5 to 4.
293 + 10 = 303. 9 tens plus 1 ten is 10 tens, which makes a new hundred.

lessons.title: Even and Odd Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Even numbers make pairs with none left over; odd numbers have one left over.
reading: Put 8 buttons in pairs. You get 4 pairs. None are left over. So 8 is *even*. Put 7 buttons in pairs. You get 3 pairs and 1 left over. So 7 is *odd*.
Here is a fast check. Look at the ones digit only. If it is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, the number is even. If it is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9, the number is odd. So 346 is even. 231 is odd.
Even numbers are doubles. 8 is 4 + 4. 10 is 5 + 5. 12 is 6 + 6. Odd numbers cannot split into two equal groups. Try to split 9 in half. You get 4 and 5, not a match.

words.d: a number that makes pairs with none left over, like 2, 4, 6
a number that leaves one out when you make pairs, like 1, 3, 5

look.title: Partners for the Game
look.text: Kai's class has 23 students. The teacher says: find a partner! Everyone pairs up. Picture the pairs standing in a row. Does someone stand alone? Now picture a class of 24. Does anyone stand alone this time?
look.prompt: Is 23 even or odd? Is 24 even or odd? How do you know?

check.why: 18 ends in 8. It makes 9 pairs with none left over. 18 is even.
31 ends in 1. Pairs leave one out. 31 is odd.

check.q: Which number is a double, like 6 = 3 + 3?
check.why: 14 = 7 + 7. It is even. 9 and 11 cannot be split into two equal groups.

review.q: What number is 5 hundreds, 7 tens and 3 ones?

review.why: 8 hundreds is 800. 4 tens is 40. There are 0 ones. So 800 + 40.
907 − 100 = 807. The hundreds digit drops from 9 to 8.
489 ends in 9, so it is odd. Numbers that end in 0 or 4 are even.

chapters.title: Adding and Subtracting Bigger Numbers
chapters.bigQuestion: How do hundreds, tens and ones help us add and subtract big numbers?

story.title: The Lemonade Stand
story.kicker: Two days of sales, two cards with numbers and one big question: how many cups in all?
paragraphs: It is a hot weekend in July. Kai and Rosa set up a lemonade stand on the corner. A cup costs 50 cents. Saturday is busy. Cars stop. Neighbors walk over. By dinner they have sold 48 cups. Rosa writes 48 on a card.

Sunday is a little slower. Clouds roll in after lunch. Still, they sell 36 cups. Rosa writes 36 on a second card. Kai looks at the two cards. How many cups did we sell in all? he asks. Rosa starts to count on her fingers. That will take forever.

Then Rosa remembers the button jar. Tens and ones! she says. 48 is 4 tens and 8 ones. 36 is 3 tens and 6 ones. Add the tens: 7 tens. Add the ones: 14 ones. But 14 ones is a ten and 4 more. So that is 8 tens and 4 ones. Eighty-four cups!

Kai checks it another way. 48 plus 30 is 78. Then 78 plus 6 is 84. Same answer. They high-five. Then Kai asks a harder question. We had 100 cups at the start. How many are left? That is a subtraction problem. And it is next.
story.think: Rosa and Kai got 84 two different ways. Why is it smart to check an answer with a second way?

lessons.title: Tens With Tens, Ones With Ones
lessons.mainIdea: To add two-digit numbers, add the tens together and the ones together.
reading: Let's *add* 32 + 45. Break each number apart. 32 is 3 tens and 2 ones. 45 is 4 tens and 5 ones. Add the tens: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens. Add the ones: 2 + 5 = 7. So 32 + 45 = 77.
Picture the rods and cubes. Put 3 rods next to 4 rods. That is 7 rods. Put 2 cubes next to 5 cubes. That is 7 cubes. 7 rods and 7 cubes show 77. The *sum* is 77.
A common mistake is to add a ten to a one. In 32 + 45, do not add 3 + 5. The 3 is tens and the 5 is ones. Tens go with tens. Ones go with ones.

words.d: to put amounts together and find the total
the answer you get when you add

look.title: Rods and Cubes
look.text: Picture 5 rods of ten and 1 cube. That is 51. Now picture 2 rods and 6 cubes. That is 26. Push all the rods together. Push all the cubes together. Count the rods. Count the cubes.
look.prompt: What is 51 + 26? How many rods and cubes do you end with?

check.why: 2 tens + 5 tens = 7 tens. 3 + 4 = 7 ones. So 77.
4 tens + 3 tens = 7 tens. 1 + 6 = 7 ones. So 77.

check.q: In 62 + 15, which two digits are both tens?
check.why: 6 is the tens digit in 62. 1 is the tens digit in 15. Add them to get 7 tens.

lessons.title: Trading Ten Ones for a Ten
lessons.mainIdea: When the ones add up to 10 or more, trade ten ones for one ten.
reading: Add 48 + 36. Ones first: 8 + 6 = 14. That is too many ones. 14 ones is 1 ten and 4 ones. Trade ten of them for a rod. When you trade like this, you *regroup*.
Now count the tens. 4 tens + 3 tens = 7 tens. Add the new ten from the trade. 7 + 1 = 8 tens. So 48 + 36 is 8 tens and 4 ones. That is 84.
The big mistake is to forget the traded ten. Then you get 74 instead of 84. Always ask: did my ones make a ten? If yes, add it to the tens.

words.d: to trade ten ones for one ten, or one ten for ten ones

look.title: Too Many Cubes
look.text: Picture 2 rods and 7 cubes. Now add 1 rod and 5 cubes. Push the cubes together. You have 12 cubes. Ten of them can snap into a new rod. Now count all the rods. Count the cubes left over.
look.prompt: What is 27 + 15? How many rods did you end with after the trade?

check.why: 7 + 8 = 15. Trade for 1 ten and 5 ones. 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 tens. So 85.
9 + 4 = 13. Trade ten ones for a ten. 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 tens. So 83.

check.q: Kai adds 46 + 27 and gets 63. What did he forget?
check.why: 6 + 7 = 13 makes a ten. 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 tens. The answer is 73, not 63.

lessons.title: Adding Three or Four Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Add several numbers by finding friendly pairs and keeping tens and ones straight.
reading: Add 12 + 25 + 18. Look for a *friendly pair* that makes a ten. 12 + 18 = 30. That is easy. Then 30 + 25 = 55. So 12 + 25 + 18 = 55.
Try four numbers: 21 + 14 + 19 + 26. Pair 21 + 19 = 40. Pair 14 + 26 = 40. Then 40 + 40 = 80. Check it: the ones are 1 + 4 + 9 + 6 = 20. The tens are 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6 tens. 60 + 20 = 80.
You can add in any order. The sum stays the same. Pick the order that makes tens. If nothing pairs up, add the tens, then add the ones, then trade.

words.d: two numbers that are easy to add, like 12 + 18 = 30

look.title: Cups Sold in Four Days
look.cite: Kai and Rosa's lemonade stand, example numbers
look.prompt: How many cups in all four days? Which two numbers make a friendly pair?

check.q: Which pair is a friendly pair that makes tens?
check.why: 25 + 15 = 40. The ones 5 + 5 make a ten with none left over.

lessons.title: Subtracting Tens and Ones
lessons.mainIdea: To subtract, take tens from tens and ones from ones.
reading: Let's *subtract* 68 − 25. Take the tens first. 6 tens − 2 tens = 4 tens. Now the ones. 8 − 5 = 3. So 68 − 25 = 43. The *difference* is 43. Check by adding: 43 + 25 = 68.
Picture 6 rods and 8 cubes. Take away 2 rods. Take away 5 cubes. You have 4 rods and 3 cubes left. That is 43.
A number line helps too. Start at 68. Jump back 20 to 48. Jump back 5 to 43. Big jump for the tens, small jump for the ones.

words.d: to take away part of an amount and find what is left
the answer you get when you subtract

look.title: Cups Left
look.text: Kai and Rosa start Saturday with 89 empty cups. They sell 48 cups. Picture 8 stacks of ten cups and 9 loose cups. Take away 4 stacks. Take away 8 loose cups. How many stacks and loose cups are left?
look.prompt: How many cups are left? Say the tens and the ones.

check.why: 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens. 9 − 4 = 5. So 45.
9 tens − 5 tens = 4 tens. The 6 ones stay. So 46.
Add the answer back: 35 + 23 = 58. It matches the start, so the check works.

lessons.title: Trading a Ten for Ten Ones
lessons.mainIdea: When there are not enough ones to subtract, break one ten into ten ones.
reading: Subtract 52 − 17. Look at the ones. 2 − 7 does not work. There are not enough ones. So *trade* one ten for ten ones. Now you have 4 tens and 12 ones.
Now subtract. 12 − 7 = 5. Then 4 tens − 1 ten = 3 tens. So 52 − 17 = 35. Check: 35 + 17 = 52. Yes.
The common mistake is to flip the ones. Some students do 7 − 2 = 5 and 5 − 1 = 4 and get 45. That is wrong. You cannot flip. Trade a ten instead.

words.d: to swap one ten for ten ones so you can subtract

look.title: Breaking a Rod
look.text: Picture 4 rods and 3 cubes. That is 43. You need to take away 8 cubes. There are only 3. Break one rod into 10 cubes. Now you have 3 rods and 13 cubes. Take away 8 cubes. Count what is left.
look.prompt: What is 43 − 8? How many rods and cubes are left?

check.why: Trade: 5 tens and 13 ones. 13 − 8 = 5. 5 − 2 = 3 tens. So 35.
Trade: 7 tens and 10 ones. 10 − 6 = 4. 7 − 4 = 3 tens. So 34.

check.q: In 71 − 25, why do you trade a ten?
check.why: You cannot take 5 ones from 1 one. Trade a ten to get 11 ones. 71 − 25 = 46.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting to 1,000
lessons.mainIdea: With hundreds, add or subtract hundreds, tens and ones each in their own place.
reading: Add 235 + 142. Draw it. Squares for hundreds, lines for tens, dots for ones. 2 squares + 1 square = 3 hundreds. 3 lines + 4 lines = 7 tens. 5 dots + 2 dots = 7 ones. So 377.
Sometimes you trade into the *hundreds place*. Add 356 + 271. Tens: 5 + 7 = 12 tens. Ten tens make a hundred! Trade. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 hundreds. 2 tens. 7 ones. So 627.

words.d: the third spot from the right in a number; it counts groups of 100

look.title: Draw It Out
look.text: Draw 3 squares, 2 lines and 4 dots. That shows 324. Now draw 1 square, 5 lines and 3 dots for 153. Count all the squares. Count all the lines. Count all the dots.
look.prompt: What is 324 + 153? What does your drawing show?

check.why: 4 + 3 = 7 hundreds. 1 + 5 = 6 tens. 2 + 6 = 8 ones. So 768.
5 − 2 = 3 hundreds. 8 − 6 = 2 tens. 9 − 4 = 5 ones. So 325.
4 tens + 8 tens = 12 tens. That is 1 hundred and 2 tens. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 hundreds. So 620.

lessons.title: Mental Math with 10s and 100s
lessons.mainIdea: You can add or subtract 10 or 100 in your head by changing one digit.
reading: Rosa sold 48 cups. Then 10 more. She uses *mental math*. She adds a ten in her head. 48 + 10 = 58. Then 10 more: 68. Only the tens digit changes. No paper needed.
Do the same with hundreds. 325 + 100 = 425. 325 − 100 = 225. Only the hundreds digit moves. Try 640 − 200. Two hundreds down: 540, 440. So 640 − 200 = 440.
Break bigger jumps into tens. 57 + 30 is three tens more. 67, 77, 87. So 57 + 30 = 87. And 92 − 40 is four tens back. 82, 72, 62, 52. So 92 − 40 = 52.

words.d: doing math in your head without writing it down

look.title: Ten More Each Day
look.cite: Example: cups sold, going up by 10 each day
look.prompt: If the pattern keeps going, how many cups on Friday? What about Saturday?

check.why: Two tens more: 86, then 96. So 76 + 20 = 96.
One hundred less. The 4 becomes 3. So 383.
Three hundreds more: 350, 450, 550. So 250 + 300 = 550.

lessons.title: Why the Strategy Works
lessons.mainIdea: A good strategy works because it keeps the tens and ones in their places.
reading: Kai adds 48 + 36 by jumping. 48 + 30 = 78. Then 78 + 6 = 84. Why does this *strategy* work? Because 36 is just 30 and 6. Adding 30 and then 6 is the same as adding 36.
Rosa uses a different way. She makes 48 into 50. She takes 2 from 36 to do it. 50 + 34 = 84. Same answer! Moving 2 from one number to the other does not change the total.
When you *explain* a strategy, say what you did to the tens and ones. Say why the total did not change. Then check with a different way. If both ways match, you can trust the answer.

words.d: a plan or way to solve a problem
to tell how you did something and why it works

look.title: Two Ways to 73
look.text: Two students add 29 + 44. Mia jumps: 29 + 40 = 69, then 69 + 4 = 73. Leo makes a ten: he moves 1 from 44 to 29. That gives 30 + 43 = 73. Both get 73. Look closely at Leo's move.
look.prompt: Why does moving 1 from 44 to 29 keep the total the same?

check.q: Rosa solves 57 + 25 as 60 + 22. Why does this work?
choices: she moved 3 from 25 to 57, so the total stays 82
she took 3 away and lost them
check.why: 57 + 3 = 60 and 25 − 3 = 22. The total is still 82.

check.q: Kai adds 64 + 23 by jumping the tens first. What is his first jump?
check.why: Jump the tens first: 64 + 20 = 84. Then 84 + 3 = 87.

check.q: Kai gets 84 one way and 74 another way. What should he do?
check.why: Two different answers means one has a mistake. Check each step of both ways again.

review.why: 7 + 8 = 15. Trade ten ones for a ten. 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens. So 85.
Trade: 6 tens and 10 ones. 10 − 6 = 4. 6 − 2 = 4 tens. So 44.
One hundred more. The 5 becomes 6. So 616.
